scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for a parent to force their 13-year-old son to play sports or join an extracurricular activity. The parent is really frustrated because the son is lazy, gets bad grades, doesn't take care of himself, and doesn't do anything unless he has to. The mother isn't helping, according to the parent, because she's enabling the son's behavior by cleaning up after him and not setting any boundaries. The parent wants to force the son into a team sport, like basketball, for a season to try to instill some work ethic and get him out of his comfort zone.

First, I need to understand the context. The son is 13, which is a middle school age. At this age, kids are still developing their identities and learning how to take responsibility for their actions. The parent is concerned about the son's laziness, poor grades, lack of hygiene, and overall lack of initiative. The parent feels that forcing the son into an extracurricular activity might help him develop a work ethic and become more responsible.

On one hand, the parent is trying to help the son by encouraging him to participate in activities that could be beneficial. Team sports, for example, can teach teamwork, discipline, and the importance of regular practice. These are valuable life skills that could help the son in the future. Additionally, being part of a team might give the son a sense of belonging and encourage him to take pride in his achievements.

On the other hand, forcing the son into an activity he doesn't want to participate in could have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment between the parent and the son, especially if the son feels that his autonomy is being taken away. If the son is forced into an activity he doesn't enjoy, he might not put in the effort or might even rebel against it, which could make the situation worse.

I also need to consider the parent's perspective. The parent is frustrated and worried about the son's future. They feel that the mother isn't doing enough to help, which adds to their stress. The parent wants to take action to help the son, but they're unsure if forcing him into an activity is the right approach.

Another aspect to consider is the son's current behavior. He's getting straight C's, which might indicate that he's not putting in the effort academically. He's also getting in trouble for talking in class, which suggests that he might have behavioral issues. His lack of hygiene and responsibility at home could be signs of a deeper problem, such as a lack of motivation or self-esteem.

I wonder if there are other ways the parent could encourage the son without forcing him. Maybe setting up a reward system for completing chores or doing well in school could motivate him. Or perhaps talking to the son about the importance of responsibility and work ethic in a supportive way, rather than forcing him into an activity, might be more effective.

It's also important to think about the long-term effects of forcing the son into an activity. If the son feels that he's being controlled, he might become more resistant to authority in general. On the other hand, if the activity is something he eventually enjoys, it could have a positive impact on his life.

In conclusion, while the parent's intentions are good, forcing the son into an extracurricular activity might not be the best approach. It could lead to resentment and might not address the underlying issues causing the son's behavior. Instead, the parent might consider alternative methods of encouragement and support that respect the son's autonomy while still promoting responsibility and a work ethic.
